clinicalPearls: A tumour showing myoepithelial differentiation arising in soft tissue and skin, outside the salivary glands and breast where myoepithelial tumours are more familiar
Encompasses a spectrum from benign myoepithelioma and mixed tumour (with ductal structures) to malignant myoepithelial carcinoma
Characteristically coexpresses epithelial markers (cytokeratins and/or EMA) together with S100 protein, and often GFAP, calponin, p63 or smooth muscle actin
A large proportion carry EWSR1 gene rearrangements, with fusion partners such as POU5F1, PBX1 or ZNF444; a subset show FUS rearrangement
Occurs across a wide age range in the limbs, limb girdles and trunk, with morphology ranging from epithelioid to spindled cells in a myxoid or hyaline stroma
Malignancy is chiefly determined by cytological atypia, and malignant tumours (myoepithelial carcinoma) may recur and metastasise
Parachordoma is now regarded as part of the myoepithelial tumour spectrum rather than a separate entity
reference.pathophysiology: Soft-tissue myoepithelioma is defined by differentiation towards myoepithelial cells, which normally combine epithelial and contractile (myoid) properties, explaining the dual immunophenotype of keratins, S100 and myoid markers. Many tumours are driven by EWSR1 gene fusions, in which a strong promoter is joined to a transcription-factor partner to deregulate gene expression, while a minority use FUS as the alternative partner. The genetic drivers overlap with those of other EWSR1-associated soft-tissue tumours, and the degree of nuclear atypia rather than the specific fusion best predicts clinical behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Epithelioid sarcoma and other epithelioid soft-tissue tumours
Metastatic or salivary-type carcinoma showing myoepithelial features
Myoepithelial carcinoma of the malignant end of the spectrum
Mixed tumour or myoepithelioma of skin adnexal origin
additionalInvestigations: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratins, EMA and S100 as the core diagnostic panel
Additional myoepithelial markers such as GFAP, calponin, p63 and smooth muscle actin
FISH or molecular testing for EWSR1 (and FUS) rearrangement
SMARCB1 (INI1) immunohistochemistry, since loss occurs in a subset of malignant tumours
Cross-sectional imaging to define the mass and assess for metastasis in atypical cases
Careful assessment of nuclear atypia and mitotic activity to separate benign from malignant tumours
redFlags: Marked nuclear atypia indicating myoepithelial carcinoma
Rapid growth, large size or infiltrative margins
Distant metastasis, most often to lung and bone, in malignant tumours
reference.prognosis: Benign myoepitheliomas and mixed tumours are generally cured by complete excision, though local recurrence can follow incomplete removal; malignant myoepithelial carcinomas, defined largely by significant cytological atypia, carry a real risk of recurrence and metastasis, and paediatric malignant tumours in particular may behave aggressively.
pitfalls: Confusing myoepithelioma with extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma or chordoma on limited sampling
Relying on a single marker rather than demonstrating the characteristic dual immunophenotype
Underrecognising malignancy because architecture can appear deceptively bland despite atypia
Overlooking SMARCB1 loss, which can mimic other INI1-deficient tumours
Assuming an EWSR1 rearrangement points to Ewing sarcoma rather than a myoepithelial tumour
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
